title: Marines storm Cape Torokina

facts.text: Just after sunrise on 1 November 1943, the 3rd Marine Division began landing at Cape Torokina on Empress Augusta Bay, midway up the west coast of Bougainville in the northern Solomons. The invasion was called Operation Cherryblossom.

The goal was ground for airfields. Rabaul, Japan's main air and naval base in the region, lay less than 250 miles away on New Britain, close enough for American fighters to escort bombers from Bougainville.
Almost 7,500 Marines climbed into landing craft, many steered by Coast Guard crews, for a 5,000 yard run to 12 beaches. The first wave touched shore at 7:26 a.m., four minutes early.
Heavy surf tossed the boats onto the wrong beaches and smashed them into each other. By midmorning 64 LCVPs and 22 LCMs lay wrecked on the sand, and three beaches had to be abandoned.
A single Japanese 75mm gun in a log bunker on Cape Torokina raked the incoming boats, destroying four landing craft and damaging ten more.
Only about 270 Japanese soldiers held the Cape Torokina area, but from 25 hidden bunkers they met the 3rd Marines on the right flank with machine gun, mortar and artillery fire.

Sgt. Robert A. Owens, 23, of Company A, 1st Battalion, 3rd Marines, placed four Marines to cover two neighboring bunkers, then charged straight into the mouth of the firing gun. He went in through the fire port and drove the crew out the back, and he was killed. He received the Medal of Honor after his death.

The 1st Marine War Dog Platoon came ashore that day with the 2nd Marine Raider Regiment, bringing 24 dogs, mostly Doberman pinschers, under Lt. Clyde Henderson. Henderson recalled, "We hit the beach and dived for cover. All of us, dogs included."
The dogs walked point to sniff out ambushes and carried messages when telephone wires were cut. A German shepherd named Caesar made repeated runs under fire and was wounded on Bougainville.

The 25th, 53rd and 71st Naval Construction Battalions, the Seabees, landed with the assault waves to start building roads and airfields at once. About 40 percent of the landing force worked as the shore party, hauling supplies off the beaches.
By the end of the day about 14,000 men and roughly 6,000 tons of supplies were ashore.
By nightfall the Marines held a line 600 to 1,000 yards inland. Behind the beaches lay a swamp with water three to six feet deep that the maps had not shown.
Early on 2 November, American cruisers and destroyers under Rear Adm. A. Stanton Merrill turned back a Japanese force sent from Rabaul to attack the landing, in the Battle of Empress Augusta Bay.
Marine Corsairs began flying from the new Torokina fighter strip on 10 December 1943, and by January 1944 fighters and bombers were striking Rabaul from Bougainville.

declassified.fact: The landing had a decoy. In late October, Marines raided nearby Choiseul to make the Japanese expect an attack there. On 2 November, PT-59, commanded by a young John F. Kennedy, pulled stranded raiders off the island and fed them canned peaches, their first real food in six days, before running out of fuel and needing a tow home.

film.shot_notes: U.S. Navy film titled 'Marines, war dogs, Seabee activity, removal wounded sailors, Cape Torokina, Bougainville Island', dated 1 November 1943. The file is the stretch from 6:15 to 9:35 of the NARA reel, re-encoded at 30 fps. File times: 0:00 to 0:18 grave markers in the beachhead (somber, avoid as an opener); 0:18 to 0:55 a long column of Marines with packs and rifles moving along the black sand beach past the camera, the best moving opener; 0:57 to 1:20 Marines working on sandbagged positions; about 2:15 a barrage balloon over landing craft offshore; 2:30 to 3:20 a 90mm antiaircraft gun crew in the palms. Earlier in the reel (not in the file): Marines with a captured Japanese flag at 0:30 to 1:00 and the war dogs at 1:15 to 1:50. The audio track is silent.

body:
Almost 7,500 Marines ran for 12 beaches through heavy surf, and a single hidden Japanese gun was waiting for them.

1 November 1943. Just after sunrise, the 3rd Marine Division began landing at Cape Torokina on Empress Augusta Bay, midway up the west coast of Bougainville. The goal was ground for airfields. Rabaul, Japan's main base in the region, lay less than 250 miles away.

The surf tossed boats onto the wrong beaches and smashed them together. By midmorning 64 LCVPs and 22 LCMs lay wrecked on the sand. A 75mm gun in a log bunker on the cape destroyed four landing craft and damaged ten more.

Sgt. Robert A. Owens, 23, charged straight into the mouth of a firing gun. He went in through the fire port and drove the crew out the back. He was killed, and he received the Medal of Honor.

Twenty four war dogs came ashore too, mostly Doberman pinschers. "We hit the beach and dived for cover," Lt. Clyde Henderson recalled. "All of us, dogs included."

By January 1944, fighters and bombers were striking Rabaul from Bougainville.
